summary:
Satellites observe every field on Earth, but no district has a hydrologist on hand to say whether a trend is real. TimeDetective is an open-source framework that lets that expert judgment travel with the data.

A user picks a variable and a place; TimeDetective is a Agentic Time Series Analysis framework that pulls NASA records (GRACE, GLDAS, MODIS, IMERG), charts the history, measures the rate of change, and labels the result descriptive, significant or robust.

The expertise lives in an ontology of playbooks distilled from academic papers and NASA product guides. We read how hydrologists and statisticians test a trend, wrote each method as a short, readable procedure that cites its source, and chained 86 of them into playbooks: the order of checks an expert would run. The playbooks also carry the expert’s caution: “significant” is awarded only by a test whose false-alarm rate we measured, and the tool refuses when the data cannot answer and it does not hallucinate.

This democratizes expertise. The data is already free and global; now the judgment to read it is too, so anyone in any village, county or taluk can ask whether their region is really changing and get an honest, plain-language answer with the evidence behind it.
details:
TimeDetective is an open-source, agentic framework that answers a plain question about a place, such as “is the groundwater under these farms falling?”, from NASA Earth data. A user picks a variable and a region. The framework loads the record, charts its history, measures the rate of change, and returns a plain-language finding with an evidence label: descriptive, significant or robust. An executor walks an expert-defined playbook one check at a time, and a single module, the critic, decides how strong the claim is. When the data cannot answer, for example a region too small for the satellites to resolve, the tool refuses and says what would change that.

The current prototype combines NASA GRACE and GRACE-FO water-storage observations, GLDAS land-model estimates, MODIS vegetation measurements, and rainfall records from NASA POWER. It includes worked investigations of groundwater in north-west India and the US High Plains, and growing-season conditions in Karamoja, Uganda. An additional workflow can retrieve historical precipitation data through the NASA POWER API. These examples show why the evidence label matters: north-west India’s estimated groundwater decline passes the project’s calibrated significance check, while a downward-looking trend in the High Plains remains descriptive.

TimeDetective’s creative approach is to make the investigation itself reusable and inspectable. We did not train a model to imitate experts; we wrote down what experts do, distilling 44 sources by hand, including research papers and NASA product guides. The result is 86 analysis skills arranged into six executable playbooks. An ontology connects datasets, methods, required evidence, and findings, so a new investigation can follow an expert-defined route without hiding the reasoning inside a single opaque answer. The core engine is designed for time-series data beyond Earth science; adding a new domain requires suitable data, definitions, methods, and validation, rather than a new claim that every dataset already works.

We built the software in Python, using pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, ruptures, and related statistical libraries. YAML and LinkML describe the knowledge structure and playbooks; Pydantic validates results; Streamlit provides the interactive interface. The project is open source, uses publicly available NASA data, and requires no custom hardware. An AI coding assistant helped develop code and documentation, but no AI model generates findings when an investigation runs. Results come from recorded data and deterministic procedures.

Our intended impact is to make statistical expertise easier to reach. A teacher, community group, water manager, or local decision-maker in a rural or developing region may be able to access satellite data but not hire a data scientist or statistician to interpret it. TimeDetective gives them a way to explore that evidence, understand its limits, and ask better-informed questions. It is designed to support expert judgment, not pretend that a chart alone can establish a cause.

Every finding names its data, assumptions, steps and sources, and every cached NASA file carries a checksum and retrieval date. The tool states its limits: groundwater is an estimate, and it names no causes and makes no forecasts. The project is backed by 313 automated tests.
